title: Right Pascal’s Triangle Pattern
description: Brute force to optimized: recomputing factorials from scratch versus a multiplicative row recurrence, then a further correctness-focused addition-only recurrence with no division at all.

blocks.text: Given a positive integer n, print the first n rows of Pascal's Triangle, left aligned, where row i, counting from 0, contains i plus 1 numbers, the binomial coefficients i choose 0, i choose 1, and so on up to i choose i.

blocks.title: Analogy: Counting Paths on a Grid
blocks.text: Picture standing at the top of a triangular grid of pegs, like the ones in a bean machine, where a ball dropped at the top can bounce left or right at every peg it hits. The number written at any position is simply how many different paths a ball could take to land exactly there, and every row can be found by adding together the two numbers directly above it.

blocks.caption: Row i holds i plus 1 binomial coefficients, growing by one entry per row

blocks.content: {"headers":["Row","Output","Why"],"rows":[["Row 0","1","0 choose 0 is always 1, the single entry that starts every triangle."],["Row 1","1 1","1 choose 0 and 1 choose 1 are both boundary values, always 1."],["Row 2","1 2 1","The middle value, 2, is 1 plus 1, the two entries directly above it in row 1."],["Row 3","1 3 3 1","Each interior value is the sum of the two entries above it: 3 is 1 plus 2, and the second 3 is 2 plus 1."],["Row 4","1 4 6 4 1","Continuing the same rule: 4 is 1 plus 3, 6 is 3 plus 3, and 4 is 3 plus 1, mirrored back down."]]}

blocks.text: No rows at all, so nothing is printed.
This problem sits in the pattern printing section of the sheet because it prints a triangular shape, but it is worth noticing upfront that its actual difficulty is entirely numeric, not geometric.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Unlike the star and gap shapes solved elsewhere in this division, this triangle's real challenge is computing correct binomial coefficients, not building visual gaps and stars, so the geometric row-classification techniques used so far do not directly apply here.

Observation 2: The raw mathematical definition, i choose j equals i factorial over j factorial times i minus j factorial, recomputes i factorial completely from scratch for every single entry in row i, even though it never changes across that entire row.

Observation 3: Testing a small example, row i equal to 4, shows each entry can instead be derived directly from the entry just before it in the same row, using one multiplication and one division, no factorial needed at all.

Observation 4: An entirely different, and even simpler, relationship also exists between rows rather than within one, every interior entry is exactly the sum of the two entries directly above it, the same additive rule already used for pascals-triangle in the Coding Foundations category.

This is one of the rare problems in this division where the optimization story is a numeric recurrence rather than a gap-and-star construction, closer in spirit to the earlier Coding Foundations problems than to the geometric shapes solved elsewhere in Basic.

For every entry in every row, compute the binomial coefficient directly from its factorial definition, i choose j equals i factorial divided by j factorial times i minus j factorial, recomputing every factorial completely from scratch each time.

items: Loop over each row i from 0 to n minus 1.
For every column j from 0 to i, compute i factorial, j factorial, and i minus j factorial, each from scratch.
Divide to get the binomial coefficient for that position.
Print all i plus 1 values for the row, separated by spaces.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: recompute the binomial coefficient from factorials for every single entry

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: factorial(x) is a standalone helper that recomputes its result completely from scratch on every single call, with no memory of any factorial computed for a previous entry.
The binomial coefficient formula is applied literally, calling factorial three separate times for every single entry, even though i factorial is identical for every j within the same row.
Values are collected into a list and joined once per row, so the row level formatting is already efficient, it is only the per entry mathematics that is not.

blocks.text: Every entry is correct, since each one is computed directly from the mathematical definition of a binomial coefficient.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n cubed), computing a fresh factorial from scratch, itself an O(n) computation, for every one of the roughly n squared entries across all rows.
Space: O(1) extra space beyond the row currently being printed.

Limitation: almost all of that factorial work is repeated needlessly, i factorial is recomputed for every single entry in row i, even though it never changes across that row. Each entry in a row can instead be derived directly from the entry right before it, without recomputing any factorial at all.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why recomputing every factorial works but is wasteful: i factorial is calculated fresh for every one of the i plus 1 entries in row i, even though it is the exact same value each time.

What is the actual relationship between neighboring entries: i choose j equals i choose j minus 1, multiplied by i minus j plus 1, then divided by j, a single multiply and divide step instead of three fresh factorials.

Why must the multiplication happen before the division: the intermediate value is only guaranteed to be a whole number after the multiplication, dividing first, or using floating point, risks truncating a value that has not been multiplied back up yet.

Can this per entry recurrence be applied across an entire row: yes, starting each row at 1 and repeatedly applying this one step builds the whole row without ever computing a single factorial.

The core idea: derive each entry directly from the one before it in the same row, using one multiplication and one division, instead of three independent factorial computations.

Within a row, each binomial coefficient can be obtained from the previous one using a simple multiplicative relationship, i choose j equals i choose j minus 1, multiplied by i minus j plus 1, then divided by j. Starting each row at 1 and applying this step repeatedly avoids computing a single factorial.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Computation","Value","Why"],"rows":[["j = 0","starting value","1","Every row begins at i choose 0, which is always 1 by definition."],["j = 1","1 times 4, divided by 1","4","Applying the recurrence once moves from i choose 0 to i choose 1."],["j = 2","4 times 3, divided by 2","6","The multiplier decreases and the divisor increases by 1 with each step."],["j = 3","6 times 2, divided by 3","4","Continuing the same recurrence, mirroring the row back down."],["j = 4","4 times 1, divided by 4","1","The final entry, i choose i, always returns to 1."]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: derive each value from the previous one in the same row, no factorials

blocks.text: This works because of a known identity: multiplying the previous coefficient, i choose j minus 1, by i minus j plus 1 always produces a value that is exactly j times the true next coefficient, i choose j, before any division happens. Dividing by j at that exact point, and only at that point, therefore always yields a whole number with no truncation, letting the entire row be built using nothing but one multiplication and one division per step.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["The multiplication by i minus j plus 1 happens before dividing by j","The intermediate product is guaranteed to be exactly j times the true coefficient","Dividing by j at that exact point always produces a whole number, with no truncation"],["The division were mistakenly performed before the multiplication, or computed in floating point","An intermediate value that is not yet guaranteed to be a whole number gets rounded or truncated","The resulting coefficient can silently come out wrong, especially for larger rows"]]}

items: value starts at 1, exactly i choose 0, before any recurrence step has run.
Each step multiplies by i minus j plus 1 first, producing a value guaranteed to be an exact multiple of j at that specific point.
Only after that multiplication does the division by j happen, preserving exact integer arithmetic throughout the entire row.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), a genuine complexity class improvement, one constant time step per entry across all rows.
Space: O(1) extra space beyond the row currently being printed.
10. Further Optimization: Building Each Row by Addition Alone

The multiplicative version above already reaches the same O(n squared) time as this final version, but it still depends on getting the multiply-then-divide order exactly right. A completely different, and arguably more standard, way to build the same triangle avoids division entirely: every interior entry is just the sum of the two entries directly above it in the previous row, using nothing but addition.
Dry run for row i = 4, using row i = 3 as [1, 3, 3, 1]

blocks.caption: Further optimization: each new value is just two values from the previous row added together

items: Every new row is initialized with 1 at both boundary positions before any interior values are computed, matching Pascal's Triangle's boundary rule directly.
Each interior entry is computed purely by reading two adjacent values from the previous row and adding them, with no multiplication or division anywhere in this version.
The previous row is retained across iterations, so the next row always has the values it needs already available, without recomputing anything from scratch.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), the same order as the multiplicative version.
Space: O(n), to keep the previous row available while building the next one. This round is not about speed, it removes multiplication and division entirely, leaving no room at all for the kind of operation-order mistake the previous version had to be careful about.

blocks.text: Pascal's Triangle is a textbook example of how recomputing a value from its raw mathematical definition, factorials here, can hide an enormous amount of repeated work. Once a relationship between neighboring entries is spotted, whether multiplicative within a row or additive between rows, that repeated work disappears entirely, and the additive version is the more robust of the two, since it never risks a division related mistake.

items: Recomputing a factorial for every entry instead of noticing that i factorial stays fixed across an entire row.
Dividing before multiplying in the multiplicative version, which can truncate a value that was not meant to be a whole number yet.
Forgetting the boundary values, every row must start and end with 1.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["n = 0","Produces no rows at all."],["n = 1","A single row containing only the value 1."]]}

blocks.text: Noticing that this is the same additive relationship used to build Pascal's Triangle by hand, each number is the sum of the two above it, is usually the fastest path to the optimal solution, and mentioning the division order pitfall in the multiplicative approach shows attention to correctness beyond just complexity.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid recomputing factorials", think: derive each entry from the one before it in the same row using one multiply and one divide.
If the interviewer says "is there a way to avoid division entirely", think: build each row purely by adding two entries from the row above, the standard Pascal's Triangle rule.
If the interviewer says "why must you multiply before dividing", think: the intermediate value is only guaranteed to be a whole number after the multiplication, not before.

items: Why does recomputing a factorial from scratch for every entry cost an extra full factor of n compared to the recurrence based approaches?
Can you explain why the multiply-then-divide order in the multiplicative recurrence always produces an exact integer?
How would you compute a single entry, i choose j, in O(i) time without building the entire triangle first?
How would this approach change if you needed every binomial coefficient modulo a large prime, as in many competitive programming problems?
Can you adapt the additive recurrence to use only O(n) total space, keeping just one row in memory at a time instead of the whole triangle?
The pascals-triangle and pascals-triangle-ii problems in the Coding Foundations category, which already established this same additive row-to-row recurrence.
Any problem computing binomial coefficients or combinatorial counts, where a raw factorial formula almost always hides a cheaper recurrence between neighboring values.
Dynamic programming problems in general, where building a row or state purely from the previous one is one of the most common recurrence shapes.
The multiply-before-divide correctness pattern, which reappears in other combinatorial formulas that are only guaranteed to be exact integers after a specific order of operations.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force factorial approach runs in O(n cubed) time and O(1) extra space. Both the multiplicative and additive approaches run in O(n squared) time, a genuine complexity class improvement, with the additive version trading O(1) extra space for O(n) in exchange for removing division entirely.

items: Pattern: a math and counting pattern, building Pascal's Triangle through a recurrence between neighboring values instead of recomputing each binomial coefficient from its raw factorial definition.

Core Idea: each entry can be derived directly from a neighboring value, either multiplicatively within the same row or additively from the row above, instead of computing three fresh factorials per entry.
Time: O(n cubed) for the brute force, O(n squared) for both the multiplicative and additive recurrences.
Space: O(1) extra beyond the current row for the brute force and the multiplicative version, O(n) for the additive version to retain the previous row.
Most Important Observation: a formula's raw mathematical definition is often the slowest way to compute it, a cheaper recurrence between neighboring values is usually available.

Interview Difficulty: easy to write the brute force factorial version; recognizing and correctly implementing either recurrence, and knowing why operation order matters in the multiplicative one, is what shows real understanding.
One line memory trick: same additive rule as Coding Foundations' pascals-triangle, each entry is the sum of the two above it.
